utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. And good afternoon to you and to everyone else. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic. Present for the Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. Ready to roll? Okay. So, Mr. Lazarevic, have you thought about reducing or expanding your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon first, Your Honour. I was having a lot of thoughts, and Your Honours would be probably be pleased to hear that I significantly reduced my cross-examination. With the assistance of our witness, I believe that I'll be able to finish it in one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good. Thank you for that. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you heard what I promised the Bench. In order to meet my promise, I would kindly ask you for your cooperation and to try and answer as briefly as possible, if possible with a mere yes or no. If you don't know or if you don't remember, please say so. These are fully valid answers. In case something is unclear please ask me and I will reformulate my question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we were discussing some events of the 13th of July in the afternoon in Potocari, and we discussed certain members of the Dutch Battalion wearing T shirts. Do you remember where we left off so that I could continue with my next question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I can see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In order to get to that part of Potocari where the refugees were and the Dutch Battalion members in T-shirts, you had to pass by the Dutch base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On passing by, you could see that there were Dutch soldiers inside the base in full combat gather with helmets, flak jackets, rifles and everything else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can add that there were two types of Dutch soldiers at that moment: some were without weapons - they are in the forefront, and others who were with weapons – they are in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On one of the shots from Potocari, which is part of the footage you made, we can see a Serb soldier in a blue flak jacket and he's addressed as Miki. I just want to show you a photograph to remind you. It is P0286 -- I apologise. 2986. It is page 16. It is a photograph marked with a C. You'll see it on your screen. I suppose you know which photograph specifically I'm referring to. For the record, we are talking about the person on the right-hand side of the photograph with a blue flak jacket. Having seen this lad and having seen that he's wearing a blue flak jacket, can you tell us this: At the moment you saw it, was it your conclusion that this flak jacket had been taken from a member of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, because of a personal experience; I had received a similar flak jacket from a French TV station on previous occasions, I didn’t have it with me in Srebrenica. But it’s a banal detail. I never thought it had been taken from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more thing. When you went towards Potocari, do you remember Mr. Borovcanin telling you that he needs to resolve something that had to do with a bus theft? Do you recall anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall anything that was formulated that way. I know there were some problems in the process of transporting of some 28.000 civilians, in my view they were being transported to Tuzla. There were dozens of buses and trucks there and you can see some of them on the footage. In any case, we were headed there and having arrived there, I realised what it was that he needed to do. He probably had to secure some water and the rest. It was quite hot. You can see the man in the jacket. He actually has a T-shirt. I know he had to do something with water and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to that topic. This was merely a possible reference to a stolen bus. Do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a bus. Something was stolen. I think it was a water tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that topic. Thank you. Once in Potocari, and I can see that from the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, it is page 19, you said that alongside the road, you saw piles of items, bags, blankets, items of clothing and such. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when we arrived, when we came out of the vehicle, around the entrance and in the part where we… where I saw for he first time such… such a large number of people who had fled Srebrenica. It was a very striking image. I've never seen so many items in one pile, in a heap, and it was a clear indication of how poor they were. A person living in a city would actually never dream of wearing such things. It was quite a shock, although as a journalist I couldn't afford to be shocked as I was doing my job. However, I do believe that I reported on it appropriately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your statement, the Dutch and Serb soldiers were assisting those people to reach the buses in as orderly a fashion as possible. This is page 20 of your statement in the English version. Did you tell that to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps I can add something. If I were forced to do something, if I were a soldier and I find myself disarmed and threatened, I certainly would not looked so relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, I found a sentence which attracted my attention. It is on page 21. You said that while you were there, you didn't see anyone being beaten, maltreated, abused or anything of that nature. Can you confirm that today as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you have an image of a victor, as you saw him in any movies or on TV, it would be somewhat different from what I could see. I didn't see a smile on Mr. Borovcanin's face or on the faces of those people there. I merely saw great fatigue. However, I didn't hear a single soldier address the people boarding those buses harshly. My thinking is such that I would certainly make a note of it in the text I produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to the topic which you touched upon before I managed to reach it in the order of my questions, on that footage from Potocari, as you also mention in your statement, page 21, there was a problem with a water tank or a water truck there. Could we please see that part of your footage? This is trial video Exhibit number P02047, the number of the video is V 000-4458.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] But I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Wait, because we have to understand as well and we need to see it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we have to see it again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or to see it because I don't think we have seen anything basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it is highly important that we see one precise moment of this tape in order to identify certain person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah but stop, I take it stop at the frame, which is not the last one that we have seen and we keep on having it on the screen because otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may be able to do this in Sanction, if perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be also better, Mr. Nicholls, because what we were seeing here doesn't have a counter, so we can't pinpoint the exact location or the exact frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record we stopped at 2 hours 28 minutes 32 seconds point 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I have to express my gratitude to my colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are always so gentle, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, on this still, we can see on the left-hand side Mr. Borovcanin, on the right-hand side we can see a member of the Dutch Battalion obviously, and between the two we see two people. I am trying to focus on the two people between Mr. Borovcanin and the Dutch soldier. My first question is this: As you said, except for Mr. Borovcanin, you didn't know anyone else in Potocari. Perhaps it's out of place but can you confirm to me that you don't know these two people between the two I mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I follow the text? I don't see it. I don't know when the interpreters are done. Yes. My answer is that I don't know anyone else save for Mr. Borovcanin. I have a comment, however, which may be of assistance. The two people in the middle have certain bands which were probably an indication from a previous operation or the ongoing operation. Therefore, they were not from Mr. Borovcanin's unit. They could easily be told apart by their emblem. In the war in the former Yugoslavia, we used to call that the local troops or those defending their home land, people who did not leave the terrain from which they hailed. Perhaps you could hear me say something about water on the footage, and then I was interrupted, indicating that I realised that there was a problem with water. You can see that on -- at the beginning of this part of the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. You saved at least two additional questions for me. I'm trying to tell you to put to you that the soldiers we saw wanted to take the water tank away, it was an UNPROFOR water tank, they tried to have it towed away by the tractor as can be seen on the footage and that that was the reason why the Dutch Battalion members protested. Does that correspond to what you remember about the situation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And there was a two metre tall Dutch soldier who seemed to be very frightened there, if I can say that. Well, in inverted commas, he seems to be afraid of the Serbs. Anyway, Mr. Borovcanin's intervention, I think, was successful because I don't have footage of when the tractor towed away the water tank. As far as I remember, it stayed where it was, so I think that the agreement between Mr. Borovcanin and the Dutch soldier probably was -- succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So from your testimony if I understood you correctly, Mr. Borovcanin went to see the soldiers and prevail upon them to leave the water tank there and not to tow it away and that that was what we were looking at and what we saw, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it appeared to me on the spot when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question about this event in Potocari or these events in Potocari. While you were there in Potocari, you did not see or hear at any time that Mr. Borovcanin issued any orders to anybody; is that correct? Am I right in observing that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, when you spoke about Potocari and said that you saw members of the Special Police Brigade there, and for reference that is to be found on page 27 of your statement given to the Prosecutor, you said you concluded that on the basis of the markings or insignia they had on their sleeves. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The design that that unit wore as a marking was very obvious. You could always see it. They were easily distinguishable from others in the field and there were far fewer of them than others, say in Potocari… As far as I remember, they were far fewer than the local people wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A couple of more questions and then we'll leave the subject of Potocari. While you were there, you didn't see any act by which the males were separated, physically separated, from their families, from the women and children, you didn't see anyone pulling people aside, to one side or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We arrived at about 2.30 on the 13th in the afternoon, and the only thing that could have happened was something that happened before I arrived. Mr. Nicholls asked me that about the terrace, the situation on the terrace, where the Muslims were sitting probably separated earlier, but had they been separated at that moment, I would have filmed that too. So they were already on the terrace and were already separated and I took some shots of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I noticed something in your statement to the Prosecutor on page 32, that's the reference, I noticed that you were surprised by the number of children there were between the ages of one and three who were in Potocari when you arrived. I'm sure you remember that part of your statement and testimony.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my first association was when talking to the geopolitician from France, the very renowned politician, Lacoste, who told me about the demographic warfare that was going on or rather how you engage in demographic warfare, that is to say large population increases in order to reach your aims, your goals. Now, I was rather shocked to see the number of children there between the ages of one and three, three to four babies, because we had been listening for the two previous years how people were dying of hunger almost, they didn't have enough to eat, so I thought that this was an unbelievable image to witness. You know how little children are all-- look nice and good looking children, these weren't children from Darfur, they weren't thin or anything, and that's what struck me because when I looked at some data and information later, there were some 5.000 to 6.000 children born from 1993 to 1995, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. But just to complete the transcript, on page 9, line 24, if I heard your answer, you said "We heard that people were living -- were dying there," whereas can we clear that up? On the transcript it's said "They were dying of hunger"?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I wasn't there of course. Some people were able to enter with General Morillon but I wasn't in that kind on those kinds of terms and American journalists entered too, but this was something that was already known in public. There were a lot of articles and stories told about Srebrenica. So if they said there was 40.000, a population of 40.000 and about 10.000 people bearing arms then 6, 7, or 8.000 which makes it a third of the people, a third of the population, were new-born babies or very small children. So if we were to analyse that, then that would not be normal in view of the tales being told about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the next exhibit that we are going to see will help us resolve some of these things and depict them so that we can gain a true image and true picture of what was happening there, and it's a document dated the 11th of January 1995. It was compiled by the municipal staff of civilian protection of Srebrenica, and it is a review of the population households, and I'd like now on e-court to have 4D127 shown, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we can zoom it a bit and just to show the witness the lower part of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Petrovic, here we can gain an impression of the age structure here of the people, the population, and we will look at the second part of the document later on. So in the last column on the right, we have the letter M, which means male, and at the top it says, up to the age of 18, and the figure there is 6.294. Can you confirm that that is so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the upper part of this table, we have the column with the gender or sex and it says Z or F for female, and the third column says or, rather, fourth column says up to 18, 5.706. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Could we now scroll the document to see the upper part? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we have the upper table, where in the first column it says, total number of population, 36.051.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, since this is a document originating from the civilian protection staff of Srebrenica and that we are dealing with the beginning of 1995 and that of course there might be some deviations from this, but regardless of all that, the situation was the following: It shows that almost -- almost more than -- perhaps more than a third of the Srebrenica population was below the age of 18. Do you agree with my observation there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, the figure that you used, 7.000 or 8.000 children up to the age of three is not precise enough perhaps.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, it isn't. But the impression was exceptionally strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to leave Potocari and move on to another area on that same day, the 13th, after Potocari, where, according to your statement, you stayed for approximately half an hour to one hour and that is on page 29 of your statement, in English, and then you said you set off to Bratunac, and along the road to Kravica, Sandici and so on; is that right? Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: From your testimony, I gathered that along a section of the road, and you called it the Kravica stream where there was that dilapidated house and a meadow across the way, that on this broader part of the road you once stopped and filmed the surrender of Muslims, as well as the members of the Special Police Brigade who were there, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you filmed on that same occasion two young men wearing uniforms, one with the insignia of the Special Brigade who says - you remember that part - "Boro, let's change the rifle -- the pistol." And then you filmed the surrender, the stream, the young man and everything else.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All those scenes were filmed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us now to look at another exhibit that we saw yesterday during your testimony, and that is P02986, page 52, please. It is a photograph, photograph D [as interpreted]. I said B, photograph B. I see that there is a mistake in the transcript and that it says D. So it should be B. You remember yesterday that you saw this same photograph and the Prosecutor was interested in something about the car. Now I'm interested in something else. When we look at this photograph now and when we see your footage, although I didn't want to go through all the footage, but can we state that this was taken from a distance and using the facilities you had you zoomed in from a distance to film this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And let me remind everyone here in court that it's a camera which is not for professional use. It's a very weak camera, the ordinary one, the number 8 type, 8-millimetre type as we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have two questions with respect to this photograph. You didn't come up close to them to be able to see who the person with the blue helmet on was talking to Mr. Borovcanin. You didn't come up close enough, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And when I looked through the camera I didn't notice anything special and the scene before that, I was near the ditch by the road with the young man who wanted to exchange his pistol with the other guy. He was very young so that's what drew my attention. You know, a journalist always wants to have an image to hold people's attention, but this was a very banal and ordinary sort of scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to ask you whether you perhaps know the identity of this person or to what unit he belonged. We can't see it on the basis of this photograph, but I'm just asking you whether you could say who that person could be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour at this point I will have to ask for the assistance again from my colleagues from the Prosecution, it seems that our Sanction system does not work, and I hope that Ms. Stewart will be able to assist me at this point because I need to show to the witness one portion of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure the Prosecution will comply. They have an indication of which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that they are already informed. [Interpretation] Just for the record, this is Exhibit P02047. It is a trial video, and on the tape it is from 024745 to 024812. So I think that that's the section that we will be showing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Please stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show you this footage, I selected that from the entire footage, because you spoke about this when you talked to my colleagues from the Prosecution, and it's on page 82 of your statement too. Tell me, please, with respect to this piece of information, what the soldier says here about the fact that 3.000 or 4.000 surrendered and then you say, "Is that exaggerated?" And then he said, "Well, yes, it is exaggerated." And then you take him back to what you were asking him. What was your impression? How credible is that piece of information, would you say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got the text on my screen to facilitate the work of our lady interpreters. Now, the text, as far as I remember, that's the figure I bandied about on the 21st of July, but these were still rumours and this is the impression gained by a man who covers just several metres along a road or in a space. And I don't think even Mladic would be able to provide you with that kind of information let alone this young local guy who is there supervising this very, very narrow stretch of road. So that's why I left it there, this part, and it speaks for itself. It shows how arbitrary this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you but for us to investigate this question in depth and bearing in mind the fact that you filmed people who surrendered on the meadow in Sandici and that you did have an opportunity of seeing those people yourself gathered in the meadow, according to your estimate, how many people were there approximately in that meadow? You went up to them and filmed them. How many people could there have been there in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my impression that it would be enough people to fill a bus load, a bus load of people, and I think that I could stand by that and if we were to take a satellite image, and they are precise to within five centimetres or even more precise, I am very surprised that that isn't a fact that has been established here in court up until now because satellites could be used and they would show that I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I was just interested in your assessment and impression so that will suffice as far as I'm concerned for the moment. And now just one more question with regards to that meadow in Sandici. You were free to film? Mr. Borovcanin never told you not to film the people in the meadow? He didn't say don't film what's going on here? Don't film the people in the meadow? Nothing like that? Can you confirm that that was so?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he did not. Well, let me remind you, as I told Mr. Nicholls earlier on, I had two experiences with that unit during the war, and I conducted myself professionally, I did my job professionally, so there was no need for anybody to supervise me in any way, absolutely no need for them to supervise and see what I was filming, if they had already given me permission to film.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I just wanted to clarify that point, but I think that that is enough. Yesterday during your testimony at page 46 of yesterday's transcript, you said that later you heard some rumours that some of the people from the meadow were subsequently killed and specifically you mentioned the person by the name of Ramo. My question is this: After everything you saw and experienced during the two days in the area, do you believe today that Mr. Borovcanin did not know what was about to happen or, rather, that the people from the meadow would get killed at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my deep professional belief, and I believe in that as a person, a human being. I don't know whether I can assist you any further except for stating this clearly. Nothing indicated that it would turn any other way. I have 29 years of journalistic experience and at that point I had some 20. I would have sensed that and I simply could not resist continuing filming if that were the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave the topic of the Sandici meadow. I have only one question concerning the part of the footage showing the bodies in front of the Kravica warehouse. We saw that two or three times yesterday. I don't think it is necessary for me to replay it again, but you also refer to that at page 236 of your statement given to the Prosecutor. I would just like to confirm a detail from your statement, if possible, of course. When you passed by the Kravica warehouse, then, on that occasion, you didn't see any of the soldiers you can see there shooting towards the warehouse, towards the windows and the entrance of the warehouse. Can you confirm to me that this is what you've already stated to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can categorically confirm that. That sequence is only a few seconds long and only if we slow it down and zoom in can we see people appearing there. As I was taking the footage, I simply wasn’t aware of any people being there. You have to understand, it’s a matter of possibly counting one, two, three… These are all subsequent viewings, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As you testified yesterday, the night between the 13th and the 14th of July, you spent that night in Bratunac. From the statement you gave to my learned friends from the Prosecution, at page 77, you said that you did not spend that night in -- or rather you did spend that night in Bratunac but you did not hear any shooting.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will leave that topic as well and move on to another one. You testified that together with Mr. Borovcanin the next day, after the events, you went to Srebrenica and Zeleni Jadar where you also filmed Mr. Tomislav Kovac. Do you remember that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, I observed a detail which may have been unimportant to you but on page 72 of the transcript you said that on that occasion, on the 14th, when you went to Srebrenica and Zeleni Jadar, a driver was with you. According to the information we have, that is the Defence, the driver of Mr. Borovcanin was on another location on the 14th driving someone else to another place, and you can see on the footage that at least three people were in the car. Do you allow for the possibility that it was someone else accompanying you that day, not the same person who was with you on the 13th but another one who was maybe driving?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. As I said, I tried to stay focused as a one-man band. I was interested in what I was seeing and as to who was driving us, that was unimportant to me. Therefore I allow for the possibility that the driver was not the same. I simply do not remember the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In responding to some of the Prosecutor's questions, when providing your statement, at page 106 of the English, you said that when you were in Srebrenica and in Zeleni Jadar with Mr. Borovcanin on the 14th, you said that Mr. Borovcanin did not brief Mr. Kovac. You thought that was quite ordinary since they were both professionals and that it would be inappropriate that some sort of a briefing would be conducted in the presence of another person. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will remind you of the footage. When we arrived there, there was a local policeman, probably the new chief. He is the one who is supposed to brief the minister. As far as I remember, Ljubisa merely greeted him, as did all of us. It was not his territory. He was not chief of police there. There was a person doing that job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood your yesterday's testimony properly, I believe at a certain point we had some problems with overlapping and translations and interpretation of everything you said. However, I think you said that once in Srebrenica, you could wander about on your own and film things and Mr. Borovcanin did not accompany you any longer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there was an interval during which you didn't know what Mr. Borovcanin was doing, whether he was talking to Mr. Kovac or anything else. That's what I conclude from your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Regarding this, just two minor things to clarify. It has to do with yesterday's transcript, and I wasn't quite sure whether everything was taken down properly. It had to do with the fact that you mentioned a certain Lukic on page 69 of the transcript. I understood that the person by the name of Lukic you referred to that person in the context of a breakfast where you were together with Mr. Kovac and Borovcanin. On page 69, it was recorded -- transcribed as having taken place in Belgrade. Can we correct that, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no breakfast in Belgrade. It was in Bratunac, prior to the departure for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I observed that and I thought this would be the best way to clarify it so that you can explain it to us. Since Mr. Borovcanin was there as well as Mr. Kovac, and the rest, those people were from the police, weren't they? And I'm asking you whether it was possible that you wrongly remember the name of the last person, that maybe it wasn't the last name of Lukic but some other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I allow that as well. However, I probably may have registered a Lukic there. Maybe I can be of assistance because I now understand what Mr. Nicholls had in mind. He had in mind the famous Lukic from Visegrad. I heard some things about him. But that Lukic or such a Lukic was not present at that breakfast. If there was a Lukic, it wasn't "the Lukic." That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe this is crystal clear now and I think it does away with the learned friend's from the Prosecution's dilemma. To conclude, I have a few questions left. You mentioned this in your statement. However, in 2002, when Mr. Borovcanin came to see you and asked you whether you wanted to provide a statement about all these events, he actually conveyed to you his request for you to give your contribution to the proceedings? Did he tell you at the time that he wanted you merely to tell the truth and nothing else? He didn't ask you to do anything else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He put it very clearly and concisely. And as I said, I answered positively, without hesitation. I wanted to help that person and I wish I could have helped more because of my impression of his character.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am convinced that my client would like to thank you personally for these words. However, I would like to thank on his behalf, though. On that occasion, you presented Mr. Borovcanin with a copy of your book and you wrote an inscription in it. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that was in the winter or spring of 2002, it could be true. I published the book "Al Qaeda, The Green Comintern Against The Judeo-Christian Civilisation." I'm proud of that book. It is a part of the congress library in Washington, and it wasn't sent there by me. I believed Mr. Borovcanin to be interested in that topic, as I was, and this was simply a gesture on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: My last question had to do with your statement to the Prosecutor. That part is on page 258 in the English. You said "If Ljubisa did anything then I should be accused as well and I have nothing to hide." Those were your words on the occasion of that interview. What was your reason for saying that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During those 40 some hours that I spent in the field, I believe there was not a trace of such a possibility. If this man were any different, I would never have asked him for such a big favour and I wouldn't have spent time with him. I can state in full responsibility here before Their Honours that if he did anything bad, committed any crime during the time we were there, please by all means keep me here and let us try to establish what happened there positively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic and together with David Josse, I appear on behalf of General Gvero, and on behalf of my client's defence I wanted to ask you a few questions. We speak the same language. However, I will do my utmost not to overlap, the same applied to Mr. Lazarevic's questioning. Therefore, please observe the same rules before you start to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Krgovic please speak closer to the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this better for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, a clarification, please. When answering one of Mr. Lazarevic's questions on page 7, lines 22 and 23, you described the Dutch soldier who was almost two metres tall, you said that he was frightened. Was that an irony? We who speak the same language understand the nuance, but it is probably not reflected in the transcript. Can you explain that in more detail, what your impression was of his appearance and behaviour?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to thank you for that, since I said in inverted commas. I said that he was beside himself, he was very frightened, and but I meant that ironically. I was being cynical. You can see the footage for yourself and you realise what I had in mind. It was just another illustration of my general impression that I did not see a single frightened Dutch soldier. I saw Dutch soldiers working, trying to evacuate those people and cooperating with the Serbs. If someone is afraid, that person behaves differently. There was a Dutch soldier drinking milk. If you're terrified, you don't drink or eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Petrovic. To move on to a different topic, when you provided your statement you mentioned that on one of those two days in Bratunac you met two people in the street. Can you tell me -- well, they seem to have been journalists. Can you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you see why it's good for me to have this piece of paper here. It is from that period. I wrote down The Independent, Peter Block was there with Braco Grubacic. Actually I meant to say The Independent, The Independent, the British daily. He was with Braco Grubacic I wrote down the title of the text published on the 21st of July; although, I believe he published some even prior to that date. The title was "Mass Slaughter in a Bosnian Field, Knee Deep in Blood." Page 46. Those were the two men I encountered. We greeted each other, since I knew Braco. He is my work mate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Braco Grubacic. He was an owner and editor of a magazine called V.I.P. Daily News. Can you tell us what sort of a magazine that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a real magazine. It's a specialised edition for foreigners in Belgrade. You have it in Zagreb, in Sarajevo, and everywhere else now, that kind of thing, giving reliable information, a digest of important information so that any foreign person can extract the most important things, and the clients of various businessmen who happen to be in Serbia and the reputation of this VIP magazine is very high. It has a very good reputation. And proof of this is that Braco Grubacic throughout the war was probably one of the most-interviewed Serbs by the western media. So what he said in analytical terms was considered to be of high quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the information he gave was reliable, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were thought to be reliable, and I read some of his articles, not all of them of course, but I can say that they are at a very high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: May I now have 6D195, please, Exhibit 6D195? Mr. Petrovic, this is an issue of that magazine. It is dated the 31st of July 1995. Are we talking about the same publication?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I haven't read this particular article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All I wanted was for you to confirm that this publication and that it deals with the person that you saw in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's now changed its address and is now on Trg Republike or Republic Square.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I don't need the document any more. I'm going to move on to another area now. You touched upon that during the examination-in-chief. We saw here, we saw your film, your footage, and I'm especially interested in your stay in Srebrenica the following day. It's the film the 14th of July during the day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now I looked at how Srebrenica appeared and how you filmed it and the locations and the buildings in the centre, the main street and so on. It is my impression watching that that Srebrenica, at least judging by that footage, was fairly well preserved, that is to say I never saw any freshly destroyed houses or visible traces of shelling anywhere. Does that correspond to the actual state of affairs as you saw it when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That -- well, since Srebrenica was something that the media focused and just like Sarajevo of course, this is a much smaller place than Sarajevo, but you remember that people said that 5 million shells fell on Sarajevo. If that had been the case, there would have been nothing left of Sarajevo whereas it still exists. Now, the interesting thing here was well the operation didn't last too long either. I think it started on the 5th or the 6th. But obviously, the defenders left everything very quickly, and my footage shows traces of hits, the hits, but they are old traces. You can see that on the texture of the surface of the buildings. But the important thing is this: In my footage, you can see something that is not the general urban image or rather you can't see the same thing that you can see in Sarajevo or Zagreb. Already in July, those people had -- had already collected all the firewood they needed for the winter and winter wasn't to arrive, it was in two or three months' time. So they were diligent people. And had there been any serious shooting and serious fighting, I would not have been able to film it in that state because there are many buildings that were intact, nothing wrong with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You reported from Vukovar and the battle ground throughout Yugoslavia, and you know what a town that has been heavily shelled and destroyed looked like. Now, Srebrenica, the way you saw it, does it look like a town that was shelled by hundreds of grenades for many, many days? Did it have that appearance? Shells, mines, anything like that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I arrived three days after that, it would be impossible to record an atmosphere like that. What I want to say is that I saw no new traces apart from the ones I showed which dated back two or three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So all reports to the effect that such a large number of shells fell on Srebrenica would be a sheer lie?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a professional journalist, if I were in an editorial office that published that and then appeared in Srebrenica I would be -- have been ashamed to show my face in Srebrenica, had that been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In response to questions from the Prosecution, and this was recorded on page -- just a moment, please. Let me find it -- 102 and 103, you described having seen, when you visited Zeleni Jadar and Srebrenica, that you saw traces of fresh shelling and that you saw some fire, that there was some fire burning. Where were those locations? You described them to the Prosecutor, you said there were things that were still on fire. So where did you see that? What location was that where you saw that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you want to go from Srebrenica to Zeleni Jadar, and the factory there, then you would take the serpentine road, and it's a very high inclination, and it's near that factory somewhere, two next door houses at some check-point perhaps or some crossroads or junction. I can't remember the details but it was several kilometres away. I don't know how far Zeleni Jadar is from the town, but certainly quite a few kilometres. So it's -- it's in the direction of where the Serb army was burgeoning and they were the defence lines that were speedily left and they took to the forest, the Muslim fighters, took to the forests, so I just -- that was the only location where I could film some fire. But in town, there were no houses on fire or anything like that. There was something else. I saw something else in -- and that was people fleeing from the houses and general chaos in the flats, and I came across some people like that on the street. But otherwise, the town was in good condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see on that footage any traces of glass, shattered glass, glass from shattered windows or anything like that. Did you happen to notice anything like that perhaps, something that your camera didn't record?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had I seen something like that, then just like any journalist, I would have seen that, and I would have stepped on glass because glass, when you see shattered glass, then you can think that there had been wartime destruction but there was no shattered glass, broken glass, or anything from some recent explosion or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I noticed was this: There were quite a few windows who had some plastic foil over them covering them, some nylon sheeting or whatever.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was probably from 1992-93, the war, and I remember when I was in Israel, as soon as there was the danger of an attack, then the windows would be taped across, and that would avoid the glass causing any damage but I'm not quite sure what you meant with your question about the glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said you were impressed by the fact or you noticed that there was this nylon sheeting over the windows.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was very noticeable in Srebrenica, for example, and of course it wasn't the Serbs who put that up in the space of two days, the ones who returned to their flats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, yesterday you discussed something with the Prosecutor, the article that you published in fact after you returned to Belgrade, and I wanted to ask you a couple of questions linked to that article so might we have the next exhibit, P469, put up on e-court, please? And may we see page 2 of that article, please? In English, it is page 2 and 3. It begins at the bottom of page 2 and goes on to page 3. Mr. Petrovic, I followed with great attention the answer you gave to the Prosecutor with respect to the source of your information for this article, and you said that for most of the statements you make in the article and what you say in the article, you had statements from eye witnesses. Now, analysing this article, I came across two pieces of information for which you did not give any source, which seemed to be a little different from the rest of your articles. That's my impression. Now, reading this as a layman, if I can say that, and you know this better than I, but usually when you write an article in most cases to give meat to the bones of the article, then you say something a bit bombastic perhaps, you make a dramatic conclusion or something like that. You give a strong impression or you give perhaps a journalistic speculation. Now, reading your articles, when you worked for other magazines, that seemed to me to be your style.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say that it's easy for Wolf Blitzer to -- well, you noticed that very well, that part of the text is a little different from the rules governing a general report. I could have made it -- put it between the lines or in an inserted section. Now, we don't have the same culture of information as you do elsewhere. That is to say politicians in our countries have not become accustomed to being a citizen service, so it's much more difficult to be a good journalist in such societies. Now, on the basis of the many pieces of information that I had from earlier periods and so on, I made a compilation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection, I just don't think the record is clear at all as to really what part of the article we are talking about. We've gone on for about a page. He's talking about "I could have put this bit between the lines," and my friend has been talking about a section and we have some page references, but I think for the record it could be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Mr. Nicholls is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still haven't come to that. I intend to come to it in just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I think we need to get back to Mr. Petrovic and re-establish the link because we interrupted him maybe a little bit, in an unorthodox manner. But anyway, are you in a position to continue from where we interrupted you, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was saying, the basic thing is that you notice this very well, that that part of the text, the part of the text that you're interested in, because the name Gvero is mentioned here, is a little different from the rest of the article. I wanted to supplement it and give it a new dimension or a different dimension for the readers' benefit. And that is the result of the various information sources I had before, with respect to Republika Srpska and so on. I was probably one of the few journalists in Serbia who spoke about that from time to time. Let me repeat again, since 2003 [as interpreted], Milosevic forbade the Belgrade media to give out detailed information from Republika Srpska, let alone make an RTS programme, Radio Television Serbia or anything like that. Now, this interview was conducted by Milomir Maric and so he released the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here you say it seems, it would appear. So in this part of the article you put all the people from the army of Republika Srpska and you place them in the Supreme Command here.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you zoom in to that portion of the text? I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. The left-hand side. It says, "it seems," "it appears that."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that to do with the definitive abolition of the enclave, "it seems that" -- I see. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move up a bit, please? See the upper half of the article? It's page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have page 3. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You put the Supreme Command, you mix apples and oranges?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do I mix apples and oranges. Is that what you mean? There is no place for civilians there, Krajisnik, Plavsic, Koljevic, but I think that Karadzic is among them there, that he belongs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another exhibit now to explain who made up the Supreme Command. Can we see Exhibit P422, please? This is also numbered 725. This is the Official Gazette of the army of Republika Srpska dated the 29th of November 1994. May we have page 2 of this document on our screens, please? Now, may we zoom in to article 3, please? And it is page 3 for the English. Mr. Petrovic, here we have the composition of the Supreme Command, the president, as the Supreme Commander, the vice presidents, the president of the assembly, the Prime Minister. May we see a little lower down, the lower portion, thank you, the Defence Minister and the Internal Affairs Minister. Now what I want to say is this, and you agree with me, that this was guess work on your part about the composition and about all these events which were -- I mean the article, your article. To put a bit of meat on the bones of your article, as you journalists like to say. Now, let's go back to Exhibit P469 now, please. Page 2. And in English it is to be found on page 9. It's a separate part. And underlined, bold letters, where you talk about the appearance of Fikret Abdic, that phenomenon. So that's the other thing that seems to appear a little different from the general way in which you write your article, and for the same reasons, that's why you introduced that part, for the same reasons as you've just explained to us, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I wouldn't do the same thing now. I see here or rather when I compare this to the previous document, I see some differences. I mention Milovanovic, Gvero, and Tolimir, and we are in agreement that they were not members of that body. That is clear as day. Nothing needs to be proven there. My mistake. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. I have no further questions and I thank you for your time. Your Honours this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Krgovic. Is there re-examination, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think there will be, Judge, a short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, how short?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd rather take the break now. I want to look for one document. And it will probably be a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll have a short break now. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, my friend, Mr. Lazarevic, asked you about the blue vest that we saw in one of the photo stills. And you were able to say that you believed it was not a DutchBat vest. I want to go back to a part of your article and ask you a question about it. This is on page 5 in the English of Exhibit 469. I'll wait for that to come up. Maybe I can just read it to you to speed things up. "The Dutch soldiers 'captured in Potocari,' were walking around bringing water, pushing old people in wheelbarrows and conferring with Serbs on what to do next. It is true that they handed over to the Serbs their quality blue helmets and flak jackets, pistols, caps and some equipment as war spoils." So my question is really very simply, can you really tell just from that still of the flak jacket whether it was a DutchBat one that was handed over or a different type?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at his jacket, if you look at the flak jacket, you will see -- well, those who were in a war knows that there are several kinds. This one is a very modest, thin jacket. I personally have a far-thicker flak jacket given to me by a French TV station when we went in the field. The Dutch soldiers had the heavier bullet-proof vests. This is not a quality flak jacket. If you go back to the still you'll see that it's quite thin. That is why I believe it didn't come from the Dutch. However, a lot of time has passed and I can't say any more. In any case, experts would be able to tell you. There are several types of vests, but this is not the Kevlar one which can actually stop bullets. A larger calibre bullet would easily go through this one. The source I'm trying to say is that it's probably a different one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. My friend also asked you some questions about number of children and the ages of people in Srebrenica, Potocari and you gave some of your views on demographics. I want to show a clip from the video, this is 2054, the raw footage, at 3 minutes 28.9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We saw there, you asking that woman questions about her -- how old her baby was and how many children she had. I'd ask you about that. And now but first go to another section of your article, that's also on page 5 where you talk about this same topic. It's on the top of page 5 in the English. Demographers will surely find it interesting the fact that there were approximately 10.000 children among the refugees, and out of that figure, around 8.000 are under three years old. "The war children," as they say, "This is what they really do, they are -- I can't pronounce probably hojas [phoen], the motherfuckers, they are completely surrounded. No food at all. They keep complaining but they go on procreating. Is that normal? Would you believe that? Now, you tell me what kind of religion is that, Islam? They made one more corps of soldiers right there in the middle of Srebrenica who will be after us in 15 to 20 years. Just let them stay as far away from us as possible, my friend, the motherfuckers." And then in the next paragraph you talk about a 14 year old girl with children. The baby we saw in the clip and the quote from your article, is that what you're talking about as demographic warfare those children were born for needs of war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quoted an opinion I heard in the field. If you look at things geopolitically or politically or demographically, I can confirm again that it was quite normal, after having seen the scene, I concluded what I repeated here today. If you are besieged and threatened with death and appearing not having enough to eat, then if I compare that to what I saw there, and the number of children I saw, that was the first thing that came to my mind, and I still maintain that it is not something ordinary to have so many children under such conditions. However, you can call that whatever you want. But ask the demographers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is there anything in your article whatsoever to show that you disagree with that quote, that you chose to include in this section about demographics?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I told you is what I think. The part you quoted is a quote. And the entire text is a documentary news report. My task was not to make conclusions. My task was to show the atmosphere, the situation which can be felt if you watch something on TV, but you cannot grasp that from reading a text. Some of my political opponents held this against me but from the point of good journalism this is an exceptionally good text since I used the so-called verism, the veracity reporting. I tried to convey the atmosphere of the moment. And this is what I tried to do as best I could for the public. I did my utmost. At that moment, I had no religious reasons to write about that. That was merely a document of the situation I found myself in, the contemporary or present history in its full meaning. It is a text that will stay for generations. That's how I see journalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before deciding to put a question or not, Mr. Nicholls, can I see the segment which will show the French ration box? It appears 24 something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we can stop here. Mr. Petrovic, you said yesterday, didn't you, that this part was filmed before Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you saw didn't you that the date of this ration box was June of 1997.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is expiry date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. That was my mistake. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I can help you, this is to remind you, this is what I brought from the front from Majevica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PETROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were giving to the God's warriors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we have come to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, but also on behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having cooperated with the Tribunal and come over to give testimony. And on behalf of everyone present here, we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I address myself to you very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was thinking about this. I still owe you something because everybody is here to unravel the truth. I have a proposal to make to your Tribunal, because a few years ago, I interviewed a colonel who was called Brunel [phoen] and who worked for the French intelligence services, and he has provided me with new information about Srebrenica. And up until now, I have never seen that anybody has shown any interest for this, which I deem is of vital importance. In the interview I published, I also have the text in French, this gentleman confirmed that around the spring of 1996, 1996, i.e. several months after the fight for Srebrenica, a group, as he said, a group of 100 or so combatants, Muslim combatants, arrived fully armed and reached the American Tuzla compound. Colonel Brunel was present as well as his British colleagues. The Americans did not enable him to be present during the interview. These people were transported or were flown to the United States afterwards. I know exactly where these people live in the United States. So would this be of any assistance to you or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not the right persons to communicate this information to. I would suggest that you communicate it to the Office of the Prosecutor or to any other person you may wish, but I don't think that -- or rather I am sure that we cannot either comment on what you've stated or act upon it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you have understood me fully. I hope you have understood that you would like to unravel the ultimate truth. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, documents? Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, number 40 -- excuse me, 469, which is the article, Mr. Petrovic wrote a few days after the events, and the other exhibit I would like to tender is not quite ready yet. It's the transcript of the Studio B footage broadcast. Now, it's synced with the video, but I've spoken to my friends on the Borovcanin team and they have told me they think there may be some errors in it and that we should talk about. So there is no objection, I think, to putting it in but we'll wait and have sort it out and that's -- that will be coming later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not tendering it now then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Because I think we may as well get it perfected first. So at this point I just wanted to put you on notice about that. It's just the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any objection? No objection. So document 65 ter 469 is admitted. Mr. Lazarevic, do you wish to tender any document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour, it's Srebrenica civil protection staff list of population and household numbers. It's numbered 4D00127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any objection from the other Defence teams? None. So it is so admitted. Make sure that the number is correct, Madam Registrar, please. Any further? Mr. Krgovic you don't have any? All right. So that closes the Petrovic -- yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we mention one, I think it was a translation rather than a transcription error? It's an obvious error, and I'm grateful to my learned friends who sit in front to bring it to our attention. It was at page 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Line 13 where Mr. Krgovic was cross-examining the witness. And it's obviously 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Instead of 2003, we should have 1993. All right. That concludes the Petrovic evidence. Now, we move to the next one. Erin Gallagher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The subject of Ms. Gallagher's testimony was the Muslim -- what we called the Muslim ID book and the Defence have been working with us, and I believe we've reached a stipulation on that book. So I don't believe there is any need, as I think you pointed out, for a witness on something that is self explanatory that we all agree on. And so I don't see any disagreements and I know there has been a lot of hard work so I think we're okay there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is nice music for our ears. However, apart from asking for a confirmation of this from the Defence teams, we would also like to know what's going to happen next, and if what's going to happen next will affect the deadline we have established for the end of the Prosecution case on which we are not prepared to budge. First of all, is Mr. Manning available to start tomorrow, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. He is, as you know, from Australia. When we saw that the Defence estimates were going to be undercut, we tried to see if we could move him but given his schedule and the -- how this was planned, that we could not get him here. We've -- we also have Colonel Kingori for after Dean Manning, we tried to see if we could get the colonel in. He was scheduled to testify in the Sarajevo state court today and -- but he was not able to because of a visa issue, so -- but he will be here next week. So next week looks good. As you can imagine we've been a bit conservative. We didn't want to jam this week too much and have the next week bump into a situation where we would have to bring somebody back after the holiday. So next week looks good but tomorrow I don't have a witness for you, but we only have Mr. Butler and Mr. Vasic for January, so we see no problem in ending when you say. Though, the one wild card is the length of the cross-examination of Mr. Butler, but I think even with a very long cross-examination we should be in pretty good shape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are a good lawyer, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I better sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I need to discuss with my colleagues. Madam, my apologies. I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have just heard that Mr. Kingori is a witness before the Sarajevo state court. I wonder whether we will get the Sarajevo testimony because I'm sure it has to do with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that? We are not in a position to answer -- give an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify. He came all the way to Europe and had a problem with Croatia Airlines and KLM airlines, and they held him in Amsterdam for a whole day and he missed his testimony date and then they deported him back to Kenya. So I hope he'll come. He says he's going to, and I guarantee he won't have that problem with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our refuge -- our port of refuge has always been Mr. Blaszczyk. Is there anything left for him to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, there are two other important exhibit books that we have been talking with the -- all the -- our colleagues about. They are similar to the ID book. They speak for themselves. But if they are going to be in contention, it would be -- it may be a good idea for you to have an investigator to help explain to you how they were put together. We haven't had the ability to talk in depth about those books with the Defence, whether or not we'll have -- we will be able to reach an agreement or not. I made a brief oral submission on the duty officer notebook but that was mostly related to the issue of whether or not you wanted the teachers edition with our comments or not. But there is a little, a more complicated issue that I have not heard from the Defence on, that not all the information in that book -- in that exhibit that we have put together, is information that comes from trial evidence or evidence of an expert. Some of it is hearsay that a -- our investigator picked up. For example, our investigator is told by a witness that their handwriting was on such and such a page. And it's our view that that kind of evidence is allowable as hearsay. I don't know if they even object. I don't know if they even disagree with the conclusion about the handwriting. If they don't, then it can come in. If they do, we may have a legal issue that we could discuss with you and/or that the investigator could be questioned on the particular point, though the investigators are coming as third persons in this case because most of them weren't involved in person with this sorts of information. So there are those kinds -- that issue on that book. We have another exhibit which is very similar to the Muslim ID book, and that's of identifications of many of these faces and soldiers you've seen along the road. Many of those IDs have been made in this Court and that book reflects those IDs so that you can see it in one sitting, though like I just described, some of those IDs are hearsay in the field IDs that have not come into court. We did this deliberately because we believe the rules of this institution allow that kind of hearsay and to bring in every person that said, yes, that's me in the video, would have added many, many more witnesses. So that's another issue. I don't know if there is any objections from the Defence on that. They've had this book for many months. We have some updated identifications which we would like to go over with them on to see if there are any issues there. But those are the two issues that I can think of and of course, Mr. Zivanovic has filed a motion regarding Dean Manning, a bit on the late side but that is an issue that I hope to have a written response for everyone tonight or tomorrow morning, which is another issue that can be dealt with. But aside from those issues, I don't think I have any testimonial issues to take up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Leaving apart the Zivanovic or Popovic motion relating to manning, we are awaiting your response to that and it will need to be decided before Mr. Manning starts giving evidence on Monday. Is it possible there are still two hours, more than two hours, until 7.00 and a whole day tomorrow. Is it possible for you to agree to have meetings and thrash these outstanding matters relating to the documents that you have mentioned and give us a clear picture, either tomorrow or Monday, if you think it's more feasible on Monday, so that we know where we stand and you know where you stand, following which, if necessary, we will have proper submissions formally or, in writing or orally, so that we can hand down a decision. But I suggest that you make use of this time like we are going to make use. If we are not sitting tomorrow, we are I think in a position to hand down three or four decisions tomorrow. We will be working, but we suggest that you do the same, and I'm not hinting that you wouldn't be working otherwise but that you try and get together and sort these outstanding matters that you have amongst you or between you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to address one of the exhibits referred to by my colleague which is the operational logbook. We have had the opportunity of already providing some submissions to the Trial Chamber in this regard. This is one where indeed we will have difficulty in reaching an agreement, and my colleague referred to one of the aspects of this exhibit, this proposed exhibit, to which we disagree. In that operational logbook, there are big brackets that are identified in colour which identifies a specific part of the book with the handwriting of a witness. If this was only based on the expert witness, for example, and it would be for practical reasons we let the Trial Chamber know that this bracket refers to what was testified by the expert witness, maybe there could be some agreement. The problem is that these brackets that have been included in the book are based on a number of different sources of evidence, from the expert witness, from the expert witness report that we have received, from the testimony of witnesses which have appeared before you, and also from statements of witnesses who have not appeared before you. And it is because it's a mix of sources of evidence that we say that these are conclusions which should not be brought before the Trial Chamber, at least until the end of the trial, when they make their submissions. So this is one where we will have difficulty agreeing. We can discuss but it will be difficult to agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. That's a further justification of having the meeting like the one I suggested. On the other hand I wish to add something. I understood the Prosecution, I think it was -- I don't know whether it was Mr. Thayer or you or Mr. Nicholls who dealt with this before, but the understanding was that it if there were difficulties on your part, and we did not opt for a preference, then the Prosecution was prepared to hand a clean translation. That's how I understood the submission of the Prosecution last time. What was being offered, and I remember you intervening, saying, "No, I had not requested that," but I think it was Mr. Haynes was also mentioned as a person that was directly interested and who had made some kind of call on the Prosecution to have these translated. So please do meet. We are open for all submissions that you may have, and it would be beneficial for everyone if on Monday we have a clear position, either common or a divided one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have discussed a little bit further, and the previous discussion that we had on this issue is still very fresh in our minds, and we are pleased that the issue has come up again. We suggest, again, as strongly as we did earlier on, that you meet and try and come to some kind of an agreement on this. If you don't agree, we would perfectly understand and we would also then be in a position to give you our position on that. I used "position" twice in the same sentence. I apologise. The other thing, Mr. McCloskey, is we think it would be appropriate at this time, since you have dropped a further witness, to have a revised outline of the remaining testimony, the remaining witnesses, schedule of witnesses, like the one you -- or the previous two ones that you have supplied, right up to the end of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And we'll get that done, and it's nice to know that it's very easy. It's Dean Manning and Kingori next week, and then January 10th it's Mr. Butler and then Mr. Vasic a week or two after that. And we'll get that down to you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
